title: A missing layer
bodyMd:
Two lake cores were used to reconstruct a volcanic eruption. One contained a thin ash layer at the expected depth; the other did not. The absence initially suggested that the eruption's plume had reached only one lake. A sedimentologist proposed another possibility. The second lake had a steep underwater slope, and evidence of slumping indicated that part of its sediment sequence had moved after deposition. The missing layer might reflect loss of the record rather than absence of ashfall.

Testing that proposal required cores from more stable parts of the second lake and comparison of layers above and below the expected ash horizon. If those neighbouring layers were also missing, the case for a gap in the sequence would strengthen. The sedimentologist's point was not that absence can never be informative, but that its meaning depends on whether the archive had a reasonable chance of preserving what researchers seek.
